title: 2 Kings 21:19–26
context: Amon continues his father’s idolatry for two years until his servants assassinate him. The people of the land execute the conspirators and make the eight-year-old Josiah king.

verses.text: Amon was twenty-two years old when he began to reign; and he reigned two years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Meshullemeth the daughter of Haruz of Jotbah.
verses.arminianNotes: Amon begins to reign at twenty-two and reigns two years. Arminian readers see a brief reign that continues his father’s path rather than turning from it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the short reign recorded with the usual regnal details. The narrative moves quickly to its verdict on Amon’s conduct.

verses.text: He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, as Manasseh his father did.
verses.arminianNotes: Amon “did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, as Manasseh his father did.” Arminian readers see Amon choosing to follow his father’s example rather than learning from it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the pattern of evil continued. The narrator’s comparison with Manasseh makes clear that Amon added to Judah’s guilt.

verses.text: He walked in all the ways that his father walked in, and served the idols that his father served, and worshiped them;
verses.arminianNotes: He walked in his father’s ways and served his idols. Arminian readers see the influence of a parent’s example, while Amon remains responsible for his own choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see idolatry passed from one generation to the next. Readers in this tradition stress that each king is judged for his own conduct, even when following another’s path.

verses.text: and he abandoned the LORD, the God of his fathers, and didn’t walk in the way of the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: He “abandoned the LORD, the God of his fathers, and didn’t walk in the way of the LORD.” Arminian readers see deliberate forsaking of the covenant God of Judah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Amon turning from the LORD. The verse sums up his reign as abandonment of the God who had made covenant with his ancestors.

verses.text: The servants of Amon conspired against him, and put the king to death in his own house.
verses.arminianNotes: Amon’s servants conspire and kill him in his house. Arminian readers note the violence of the palace coup, which the text records without stating the conspirators’ motives.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the narrative recording the assassination soberly. Readers in this tradition avoid speculating about the reasons behind the conspiracy, since the text gives none.

verses.text: But the people of the land killed all those who had conspired against King Amon; and the people of the land made Josiah his son king in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: The people of the land kill the conspirators and make Josiah king. Arminian readers see the community acting to preserve the Davidic succession.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s providence preserving David’s line through the people’s action. The verse introduces Josiah, whose reign will bring reform.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Amon which he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of Amon’s acts are recorded in the chronicles of the kings of Judah. Arminian readers see the standard closing formula, marking the end of a short and unfaithful reign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the narrator referring to fuller records. The brief account of Amon underscores that his reign added nothing to Judah’s faithfulness.

verses.text: He was buried in his tomb in the garden of Uzza, and Josiah his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Amon is buried in the garden of Uzza, and Josiah reigns. Arminian readers see the narrative turning toward hope as a new king takes the throne.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the transition to Josiah’s reign. The burial note repeats the location used for Manasseh, linking father and son.
